overview.title: Deep learning models struggle to adapt to novelty
overview.subsection: 19.1.1 Deep learning models struggle to adapt to novelty
overview.main_topic: Why curve-fitted models behave like static databases that retrieve familiar patterns but fail on novel inputs, illustrated with ImageNet, LLM in-context learning, the figure 19.1 puzzle and the 'steel vs. feathers' trick question.
overview.central_idea: A deep learning model is a parametric curve frozen after training: a static, backward-looking database of patterns. It excels at retrieval of familiar patterns but is inherently poor at adaptation, so its success on a problem depends on familiarity, not on difficulty.
overview.importance: This is the first and, in the author's framing, most fundamental limitation; it motivates the chapter's argument that scale alone won't produce general intelligence (section 19.2) and the focus on on-the-fly adaptation (section 19.3).
learning_objectives: Explain the 'parametric curve as static database' view of deep learning.
Distinguish training time from inference time and why frozen parameters limit adaptation.
Describe the leopard-print sofa and 'heavier: 10 kilos of steel or 1 kilo of feathers' failures.
State the author's claim about in-context learning and the role of familiarity vs. complexity.
prerequisites: Deep learning as curve fitting on a data manifold (p.170).

summary:
Section 19.1.1 starts from a compact characterization: deep learning models are **big parametric curves fitted to large datasets**. This is the source of their power (easy to train, scales well in model and data size) and of significant weaknesses, since curve fitting has inherent limitations.

First, a parametric curve only *stores* information: it is a kind of **database** (recalling the "interpolative database" view of Transformers from chapter 15). Second, this database is **static**: parameters are set during a distinct training phase and frozen for inference. The only thing you can do with a static database is retrieval, which is exactly what deep learning excels at: recognizing or generating patterns highly similar to training data. The flip side is that models are inherently poor at **adaptation**: the database is backward-looking, and inputs outside the training distribution make the model break down. Example: an ImageNet model classifies a leopard-print sofa as a leopard.

The same holds for the largest generative models. Despite claims about **in-context learning**, the author argues that LLMs mostly fetch vector functions memorized during training (millions of mini text-processing programs collected through next-token prediction) and reapply them; given something with no direct equivalent in training data, they are helpless. The puzzle in figure 19.1 (p.590) is easy for people yet, the author states, unsolved by any state-of-the-art LLM or vision-language model at the time of writing. LLM performance depends on **familiarity, not complexity**.

Even tiny variations of familiar patterns cause failures: for months after ChatGPT's release, asked "What's heavier, 10 kilos of steel or one kilo of feathers?", it answered that they weigh the same, because the canonical trick question (one kilo each) appears many times online. The explanation continues on p.590.

paragraphs.excerpt: Deep learning models are big, parametric curves fitted to large datasets.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Deep learning models are big parametric curves fitted to large datasets. That makes them easy to train and scalable in model and data size, but curve fitting also has inherent limitations.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A model is a function $f_\theta(x)$ with a fixed form and many parameters $\theta$, adjusted by gradient descent to pass close to training points. Its strengths and weaknesses both come from this one mechanism.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets up the rest of the section: every limitation is traced back to 'curve fitting'.

terminology.meaning: A function whose shape is determined by a fixed set of learned parameters.

connections: p.170: chapter 5 described a deep learning model as a very high-dimensional curve fitted with gradient descent.

paragraphs.excerpt: First and foremost, a parametric curve is only capable of information storage
paragraphs.what_it_says: A parametric curve can only store information; it is a kind of database (cf. Transformers as an 'interpolative database' in chapter 15). Crucially, it is static: parameters are fixed after training and the frozen model is used at inference.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'Database' here means a store of patterns that can be queried and interpolated, not a lookup table of exact records. 'Static' means nothing in the model changes when it encounters new data at inference time.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: If the model cannot change at inference, all its competence must be acquired in advance.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: techniques such as fine-tuning or test-time training do change parameters after deployment; the chapter returns to this idea as 'test-time adaptation' (section 19.3.6).

terminology.meaning: The phase where parameters are learned vs. the phase where the frozen model makes predictions.
The book's chapter 15 description of Transformers as storing patterns and interpolating between them.

connections: p.630: chapter 20 mentions the turn toward test-time adaptation.

paragraphs.excerpt: The only thing you can do with a static database is information retrieval.
paragraphs.what_it_says: A static database supports retrieval, which is exactly what deep learning excels at: recognizing or generating patterns similar to those seen in training. But models are inherently poor at adaptation: the database fits past data and can't handle a changing future. Out-of-distribution inputs make them break down; an ImageNet model calls a leopard-print sofa a leopard.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The sofa example shows the model relying on the strongest familiar cue (texture) because sofas with that texture were absent from training. Nothing in the model can notice 'this is new' and reason about it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It warns that strong benchmark accuracy says little about behavior on situations the training data did not cover.
paragraphs.technical_idea: This is the distribution-shift problem: generalization guarantees come from inputs resembling the training distribution.

terminology.meaning: The range of inputs represented in training; inputs outside it are 'out of distribution'.
Changing one's behavior to handle genuinely new situations.

paragraphs.excerpt: This also applies to the largest of generative models.
paragraphs.what_it_says: LLMs used for programming and reasoning-like tasks provide extensive evidence of this. Despite claims about in-context learning, the author argues they fetch memorized vector functions and reapply them; next-token prediction on web-scale text yields millions of mini text-processing programs that prompts can reuse, but a problem with no direct equivalent in the training data leaves them helpless.
paragraphs.what_it_means: On this view, a prompt with examples does not teach the model a new skill; it selects among skills already stored in the weights. 'Vector functions' refers to transformations encoded in the model's latent space.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It reframes impressive LLM behavior as broad retrieval, which predicts failure on truly novel tasks.
paragraphs.technical_idea: This is the author's position, stated strongly ('overwhelming evidence'). Others in the field interpret in-context learning as partly genuine learning; the reader should treat it as an argued thesis, which the chapter develops further in 19.2.

terminology.meaning: An LLM's ability to perform a task from instructions or examples in the prompt, without weight updates.
The LLM training objective of predicting the next token from the preceding ones.

connections: p.593: transformers fail to learn exact addition despite many examples.

concepts.name: Model as static (interpolative) database
concepts.definition: The view that a trained deep learning model stores patterns from its training data in fixed parameters and can only retrieve and interpolate them.
concepts.intuition: A huge, cleverly indexed library that can blend nearby books but never write a genuinely new one.
concepts.technical: Parameters are fixed after training; inference evaluates the fitted curve $f_\theta$ at new inputs, which works well near the training manifold.
concepts.significance: Explains both deep learning's strength (retrieval) and weakness (adaptation).
concepts.example: An ImageNet model labeling a leopard-print sofa a leopard.
concepts.misconception: 'Database' does not mean the model memorizes exact examples; it stores generalizable patterns, but only locally generalizable ones.

concepts.name: Adaptation to novelty
concepts.definition: The ability to handle situations not represented in prior experience.
concepts.intuition: Solving a puzzle type you have never seen, rather than recognizing one you have.
concepts.technical: Requires changing behavior at inference time; a frozen curve cannot do this by itself.
concepts.significance: The author identifies it as what deep learning lacks and what intelligence is about (sections 19.2-19.3).
concepts.example: Figure 19.1's puzzle, easy for humans, unsolved by LLMs at the time of writing.
concepts.misconception: Bigger training sets don't solve it; they only make fewer situations novel.

concepts.name: In-context learning
concepts.definition: An LLM's apparent ability to pick up a task from examples in its prompt without weight updates.
concepts.intuition: Showing a few worked examples and expecting the pattern to be continued.
concepts.technical: The author's account: the prompt selects and reapplies 'vector functions' memorized during training.
concepts.significance: Central to claims that LLMs can learn new skills; the author disputes this interpretation.
concepts.example: Few-shot prompting for a text-formatting task.
concepts.misconception: That it is equivalent to learning a genuinely new skill; per the author, it works only when the skill already exists in the model.

deeper.title: Familiarity vs. complexity: two different axes
deeper.body:
Picture tasks on two axes: *complexity* (how many steps a human needs) and *familiarity* (how close the task is to the training data). The author's claim is that model success is predicted by the second axis, not the first:

- complex but familiar (e.g. common programming tasks): LLMs often do well;
- simple but novel (figure 19.1, the 10-kilo variant): LLMs fail.

For humans, success tracks mostly complexity. This mismatch is why model failures can look absurd to people.

deeper.title: A library analogy
deeper.body: Imagine a librarian who has read every book in an enormous library but cannot learn anything after the doors close. Ask for something close to a book on the shelves and you get an excellent answer, even a blend of several books. Ask a question that superficially resembles a famous riddle and you get the riddle's famous answer, even if your numbers differ. Ask for something unlike any book, and the librarian has nothing to retrieve. This is the 'static database' picture of the page; the analogy is ours, not the book's.

visualizations.title: Train once, then freeze: why novelty breaks the model
visualizations.why: Diagrams the page's argument: parameters are fixed at training time, so inference can only retrieve; familiar inputs succeed, novel ones fail.

misconceptions.claim: If an LLM can solve hard problems, it can certainly solve easy ones.
misconceptions.correction: The author argues success depends on familiarity, not complexity: a simple novel puzzle can defeat a model that handles complex familiar tasks.

misconceptions.claim: Few-shot examples teach an LLM a new skill.
misconceptions.correction: On the author's account, they mostly select a skill already memorized during training.

misconceptions.claim: The 'database' view means models memorize training examples verbatim.
misconceptions.correction: It means they store patterns and interpolate between them; the issue is that they cannot adapt beyond them.

takeaways: Deep learning models are parametric curves: easy to train and scalable, but limited by curve fitting.
A trained model is a static, backward-looking database: great at retrieval, poor at adaptation.
The author argues LLM in-context learning mostly reapplies memorized functions.
Model success tracks familiarity, not complexity; small twists on familiar questions cause failures.

questions.question: According to the page, why are deep learning models inherently poor at adaptation?
options: Because they have too few parameters
Because their parameters are frozen after training, making them a static database
Because they are trained with gradient descent, which is slow
questions.answer: Because their parameters are frozen after training, making them a static database
questions.explanation: The page ties the weakness to the static, backward-looking database. Parameter count, training speed and modality are not the stated reasons.

questions.question: What does the leopard-print sofa example illustrate?
questions.answer: That a model breaks down on inputs outside its training distribution: an ImageNet model labels the sofa a leopard because sofas (with such a texture) were not in its training data.
questions.explanation: Given as the example of a model failing out of distribution.

questions.question: What does the author mean by saying an LLM's ability 'has nothing to do with problem complexity, and everything to do with familiarity'?
questions.answer: Whether an LLM solves a problem depends on how closely it resembles patterns in its training data, not on how hard it is; simple novel problems can defeat it.

questions.question: Why did ChatGPT answer that 10 kilos of steel and one kilo of feathers weigh the same?
questions.answer: The classic trick question ('one kilo of steel or one kilo of feathers?') with the answer 'the same' appears many times online; the model retrieved that memorized answer instead of reading the changed quantity.
questions.explanation: The page explains it as a failure on a tiny variation of a frequently seen pattern.

questions.question: How does the author explain what LLMs do during 'in-context learning'?
options: They update their weights from the prompt
They fetch vector functions memorized during training and reapply them
They run a symbolic search over programs
questions.answer: They fetch vector functions memorized during training and reapply them
questions.explanation: Stated on the page. LLMs do not update weights in context; symbolic search and external databases are not mentioned here.
